title: Shoulder Dystocia: Emergency Manoeuvres and Neonatal Assessment

evidenceAudit.scope: Emergency manoeuvres, team call, documentation and neonatal and maternal consequences of shoulder dystocia, from the NHS Lanarkshire (Wishaw General Hospital) guideline 2022.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The RCOG Green-top Guideline 42 and any Saudi obstetric guideline were not opened.

The opened guideline contains no dedicated neonatal resuscitation protocol and no debrief section; neonatal assessment beyond call-out, cord gases, Apgar score and brachial plexus injury awareness is not specified.
No fixed time limit for individual manoeuvres is given.
The Scottish emergency call number (2222) is local; use the Saudi hospital's obstetric emergency call.
Postpartum haemorrhage drug doses are not given; use the local haemorrhage protocol.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: The anterior shoulder (less often the posterior) catches on the maternal symphysis pubis or sacral promontory after the head is delivered. Reported incidence is 0.58% to 0.70%; by birth weight it is 0.3% under 4000 g, 4.7% for 4000–4500 g and 9.4% above 4500 g. Cord pH falls about 0.04 units per minute after the head is delivered, so about 0.28 units over 7 minutes; resuscitation becomes harder below pH 7. Risk of significant hypoxic injury is small when the head-to-body interval is under 5 minutes in a previously well fetus. Brachial plexus injury is the main neonatal complication (about 1 in 2300 UK births permanent); Erb's palsy is the most common type.

symptoms: Cephalic delivery in which the shoulders do not deliver after gentle downward traction.
physicalSigns: Shoulders fail to deliver with routine axial traction after the head.
redFlags: Head-to-body interval approaching or above 5 minutes.
Excessive traction on the fetal head, fundal pressure or downward traction.
Postpartum haemorrhage after delivery (uterine atony in about 11%) and third- or fourth-degree tear (3.8%).
precipitants: Fetal macrosomia, maternal obesity, diabetes, increased maternal age, previous shoulder dystocia.
Prolonged first or second stage, assisted vaginal delivery, post-term pregnancy.
Risk factors have low predictive value and are not independent.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Commonest form; shoulder caught on the symphysis pubis.
Less often the posterior shoulder catches on the sacral promontory.

clinicalManagement.title: Call for help and stop pushing
actions: Use the hospital's obstetric and neonatal emergency call.
Summon additional midwives, an obstetrician, a senior neonatologist, a neonatal midwife or nurse and an anaesthetist.
Appoint a leader and one timekeeper; discourage maternal pushing.

clinicalManagement.title: First-line manoeuvres
actions: McRoberts' manoeuvre: flat supine, buttocks at the bed end, thighs flexed onto the abdomen.
Suprapubic pressure: continuous from the back of the anterior shoulder; try a rocking motion if continuous pressure fails.
Consider episiotomy at any stage; check a whole hand can enter the sacral hollow.

clinicalManagement.title: Internal and positional manoeuvres
actions: Posterior arm delivery: hand into the sacral hollow, rotate to an oblique position, sweep the posterior arm across the chest.
Roll the woman onto all fours if mobile; internal manoeuvres can be done in this position.

clinicalManagement.title: Last resort
actions: Cleidotomy (clavicle fracture), Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement and caesarean section) or symphysiotomy.
Never use excessive force or traction on the head, fundal pressure or downward traction.

clinicalManagement.title: After delivery
actions: Neonatal team assessment; take paired cord gases and record the Apgar score.
Anticipate postpartum haemorrhage; assess and repair maternal trauma.
Complete the proforma; explain events to the parents; submit the incident report.

medicationPlan.note: No medicine is prescribed in the opened guideline for shoulder dystocia itself. Use the local postpartum haemorrhage protocol if bleeding occurs.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Cephalic delivery requiring additional obstetric manoeuvres to release the shoulders after gentle downward traction fails.
Significant hypoxic injury risk is small when the head-to-body interval is under 5 minutes; cord pH falls about 0.04 per minute.

teaching.scope: Emergency manoeuvres, team call, documentation and neonatal and maternal consequences of shoulder dystocia, from the NHS Lanarkshire (Wishaw General Hospital) guideline 2022.
learningObjectives: Perform manoeuvres in a structured order.
Document and debrief; anticipate neonatal and maternal complications.
pitfalls: Delay in calling the full team.
keyPoints: Head-to-body interval under 5 minutes keeps hypoxic injury risk small.
Fundal pressure and downward traction are inappropriate.

patientEducation: Explain to parents what happened, the manoeuvres used and any risk of arm weakness.
Explain follow-up for the baby and the mother.
lifestyleAndDiet: Postnatal care as for any traumatic delivery, with perineal care advice.
mdtReferrals: Obstetrics; midwifery; neonatology; anaesthesia; physiotherapy or paediatric follow-up for brachial plexus injury; risk management.
dischargeCriteria: Mother and baby stable; baby examined by neonatal team; documentation complete and parents informed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Postnatal review for perineal trauma; paediatric follow-up for any brachial plexus injury; risk review of the event.
